title: Lord of the Sabbath and the Sermon on the Plain
summary: Two Sabbath disputes, over grain picked in a field and a withered hand healed in a synagogue, deepen the conflict with the Pharisees. After a night of prayer Jesus chooses twelve apostles, then comes down to a level place and teaches a great crowd: blessings on the poor, the hungry, the weeping, and the hated, woes on the rich and comfortable, and a call to love enemies, show mercy as the Father does, and build life on his words.
story: Chapter 5 brought the first objections from the Pharisees over forgiveness and table company. Now the question moves to the Sabbath, the most visible mark of Jewish faithfulness, and by verse 11 his opponents are discussing what to do to him. Against that rising hostility Jesus forms a new community: twelve apostles, a number that recalls the twelve tribes of Israel, signaling that he is gathering God's people anew. The sermon that follows is his instruction for that community, the way of life that belongs to the kingdom he announced in Nazareth. It is the longest block of teaching so far in Luke.
historical:
The Sabbath, the seventh day of rest commanded in the Ten Commandments, had become by the first century a defining sign of Jewish identity under foreign rule. Jewish teachers debated at length what counted as forbidden work; the Mishnah, a collection of rabbinic rulings written down around AD 200, lists thirty-nine categories of work, among them reaping and threshing. Picking grain from a neighbor's field was itself allowed by Deuteronomy 23:25; the charge was that rubbing out kernels on the Sabbath amounted to harvesting. Healing a non-urgent condition was also widely viewed as work, though saving life overrode the Sabbath.

The list of the Twelve also appears in Mark 3:16-19, Matthew 10:2-4, and Acts 1:13. Luke's Judas son of James seems to be the same person Mark and Matthew call Thaddaeus. Simon is called the Zealot, which may mean he was zealous for the Law or connected to the militant resistance to Rome; the organized party known as the Zealots appears in Josephus only in the years of the revolt of AD 66 to 70, so the earlier sense is uncertain. The crowd includes people from Tyre and Sidon, Gentile coastal cities to the northwest, a hint of the wider reach of Jesus' message.
cultural:
An apostle (from the Greek for one sent) was an authorized messenger who represented the sender. Choosing twelve was a symbolic act any Jewish hearer would recognize. In the sermon, a strike on the cheek was an insult more than an injury, a public humiliation. The cloak was the outer garment that also served as a blanket, and the tunic the garment worn underneath; to give both left a person nearly bare. Lending in village life created ties of obligation, and kindness was expected to be repaid, which is why Jesus' call to lend expecting nothing cut against ordinary reciprocity.

The image in verse 38 comes from the grain market: a generous seller filled the measure, pressed it down, shook it to settle it, and let it overflow into the buyer's lap, the fold of a long robe gathered at the belt and used as a pocket. The closing parable fits the land's wadis, dry stream beds that could suddenly fill with torrents after winter rain, sweeping away anything built on loose soil.
literary: The sermon has close counterparts in Matthew's Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5-7), though Luke's is much shorter and set on a level place after Jesus comes down from the mountain. Luke has four blessings, each matched by a woe, in sharp parallel: poor and rich, hungry and full, weeping and laughing, hated and praised. Matthew has nine beatitudes and no woes, and his wording is sometimes more inward (poor in spirit, hungering for righteousness). Scholars explain the relationship in different ways: Jesus may have given similar teaching on many occasions, which the evangelists recorded separately; or both drew on a common collection of sayings, often called Q, and shaped it for their readers; or Luke abbreviated a single sermon. The sermon moves from blessing and woe (20-26) to love of enemies (27-38), to judging and fruit (39-45), and ends with a parable of two builders (46-49), as Matthew's does.

outline.t: A withered hand healed on the Sabbath
A night of prayer and the choosing of the Twelve
Crowds gather on a level place
Love your enemies; be merciful as your Father
Blind guides, specks and beams, trees and fruit

doctrines.note: The kingdom of God belongs to the poor and brings a great reversal: the hungry filled, the weeping laughing, the comfortable emptied. Its ethic reflects its King, who is kind to the ungrateful and wicked.
Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath but claims to be its Lord and shows its purpose: to do good and to save life. The Law's intent is love, and the Son of Man interprets it with authority.
Jesus forms a people around himself, with twelve apostles as its foundation. The sermon describes their common life, marked by mercy, generosity, and refusal to judge.

words.note: Makarios, blessed or fortunate. It is not a wish but a declaration about someone's true condition before God. Jesus pronounces the poor and grieving blessed, not because their suffering is good, but because God's kingdom is theirs.

Ouai, woe, a cry of grief and warning used by the prophets. The woes are not curses so much as laments over people whose comfort has already been fully paid out and who have nothing further to receive.

Oiktirmon, merciful or compassionate. In the Greek Old Testament it describes God, who is merciful and gracious. Matthew's parallel says be perfect as your Father is perfect; Luke's wording puts mercy at the center of what it means to resemble God.
Echthros, enemy. The word covers personal and national enemies alike. In a land under Roman occupation, and with neighbors in bitter disputes, love for enemies was a startling command.

christ: Jesus claims to be Lord of the Sabbath, a day God himself instituted. He spends a night in prayer before choosing the Twelve, as he prays before every turning point in Luke. The crowds press to touch him because power goes out from him. In the sermon he speaks with his own authority and calls himself the one people address as “Lord, Lord”, whose words are the rock for a life. His blessing on those hated because of the Son of Man links discipleship to him personally. And the ethic he teaches, loving enemies, blessing those who curse, praying for mistreatment, is the life he will live out at the cross, where he prays for those crucifying him (Luke 23:34).

hard.q: Did Jesus mean these commands literally: give to everyone who asks, never demand your goods back, turn the other cheek?
hard.a:
Christians have long disagreed about how to apply these words. One tradition, strong among Anabaptists and other peace churches, takes them as a direct rule for followers of Jesus, including refusing to use violence even in defense or in war. Another, reaching back to Augustine in the early fifth century, holds that they govern a disciple's personal response to wrong and forbid revenge, but do not forbid the proper use of force by governments to protect the weak, which Paul describes in Romans 13. Many readers note that Jesus often speaks in vivid, even hyperbolic, images to overturn instinct, and that in the same Gospel he rebukes the high priest's servant (John 18:23 records it) rather than literally offering the other cheek.

On poverty, some read Luke's blessings as God's special concern for the economically poor, and others as describing the pious poor of the Old Testament who depend on God, a sense close to Matthew's poor in spirit. The text itself suggests both: Luke's Gospel repeatedly warns about wealth and lifts up the poor, yet the blessing is spoken to disciples who have left everything for Jesus. Whatever the application, the commands are not less than a refusal of revenge and a generosity that resembles the Father's.

questions: Which of the four woes speaks most directly to your own situation, and how do you respond to it?
Jesus grounds love for enemies in God's kindness to the ungrateful and wicked. How does remembering God's kindness to you change how you treat someone who has wronged you?
The two builders both heard Jesus' words; only one acted on them. What is one word of Jesus you know well but have not built on?
